items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Like the late great Ben Webster, Don Byas, Stuff Smith, Rex Stewart, Benny Carter lived in Europe for years.

ctx.x: It’s been a great gift of our country to the world.

Oh, yes, to the world. He was, he played, I don’t think he missed any place on this earth playing. He played just about every place, and played for royalty, they appreciated him over there very much. In fact the Europeans appreciate jazz music more than Americans, although it’s an American art form. But it’s appreciated more in Europe. And as you know, a lot of the musicians have migrated to Europe because they appreciate them more then they do here in America. Like the late great Ben Webster, Don Byas, Stuff…

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Bill Coleman, Stuff Smith, Kenny Drew, Kenny Clarke, Johnny Griffin is still living but he’s still over there in Europe.

ctx.x: Bill Coleman, Stuff Smith, Kenny Drew, Kenny Clarke, Johnny Griffin is still living but he’s still over there in Europe. You get some much, you’re appreciated so much over there.
Were you ever tempted to settle there permanently?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Stuff Smith was in that band, yeah.

ctx.x: Stuff Smith was in that band, yeah. Snuff Smith was in that band. Alphonso Trent, he got sick up in Bangor, Maine, up there, they were doing one-nighters. So he went back to Ft. Smith, Arkansas. So the band came through Columbus, Ohio and broke up. So the Jeter-Pillars was the one --, Jeter was an alto saxophone player and Pillars was a tenor player. They decided they would get the band going, you know.
They were both in Trent's band, I see.
